title: People Whose List of Favorite Companies Is Not a Subset of Another List
statement:
Person `i` (counting from 0) likes the companies named in `favoriteCompanies[i]`. Return, sorted from smallest to largest, the index of every person whose list is **not** contained in the list of some other single person: that is, for every other person `j`, at least one company of person `i` is missing from `favoriteCompanies[j]`.

The names inside one list are distinct, and no two people like exactly the same set of companies (even if their lists are in different orders).
constraints: The names inside each list are distinct
No two lists hold the same set of names
Names contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Person `i` drops out exactly when some single other list contains all of `i`'s companies. Searching a list with `indexOf` costs O(m) per name, so turning each list into a hash set first makes every "does `j` like this company?" check O(1). Then simply try every pair `(i, j)`.

Because no two people share the same set, a list can only sit inside a strictly **larger** list. That lets us skip every `j` whose set is not bigger than `i`'s, which also skips `i` itself.

## Approach

1. Build `sets[i] = new Set(favoriteCompanies[i])` for every person.
2. For each `i`, look at every other `j` until one covers `i`. Skip `j` when `sets[j]` is not larger than `sets[i]`.
3. `covered` is true when every name of `i` is found in `sets[j]`.
4. If no `j` covers `i`, push `i` to `result`. Indices are visited in order, so `result` is already sorted.

## Example 1, step by step

Sizes are 3, 2, 2, 1, 1. Person 0 has the largest list, so nothing covers it: keep 0. Person 1 (`google, microsoft`) is checked only against person 0, which lacks `microsoft`: keep 1. Person 2 (`google, facebook`) is inside person 0's set: drop. Person 3 (`google`) is inside person 0's set: drop. Person 4 (`amazon`) is in no larger list: keep. Result `[0, 1, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · m) set lookups, where n is the number of people and m the longest list (each lookup hashes a name of at most 20 letters).
- Space: O(total names) for the sets.

## Pitfalls

- Covered by the **union** of several lists does not count: `["a","c"]` survives next to `["a","b"]` and `["c","d"]`.
- Compare whole names, not substrings: `"ab"` is not inside `["abc","b"]`.
- Do not compare a person with themselves; the size test `<=` already excludes `j === i`, but the explicit check keeps the intent clear.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sets[i]` | person `i`'s companies as a hash set |
| `i` | the person being tested |
| `j` | a candidate person whose list may contain `i`'s |
| `covered` | whether some `j` contains all of `i`'s companies |
| `result` | indices of people who are not covered, in increasing order |

narration.2: Turn every list into a hash set so membership checks take constant time.
narration.4: Test each person i in increasing order.
narration.5: Assume nobody covers person i until we find someone who does.
narration.6: Try every other person j, stopping as soon as one covers i.
narration.7: Skip i itself and any list that is not strictly larger; equal sets are ruled out, so only a larger list can contain i's.
narration.10: Person j covers i when every one of i's companies is in j's set.
narration.16: Indices were added in order, so the list is already sorted.
